1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle. But after his departure they were tempted by false apostles, to be turned to the law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to the faith of truth, writing to them from Ephesus. Paul, an apostle. By the name of his office he strikes terror. Not of men. Understand: of apostles, as certain pseudo-apostles chosen and sent by the Jews. Neither by man. But by Jesus now risen. Who taught not as man teaches men little by little, but the whole at once by the Spirit: so that he is greater in that in which he seemed less. For the other apostles seemed greater because they were first. This one the least, because last. But from this he appears more worthy: because the first were appointed through Christ still partly man, that is mortal. But Paul, the last, through Christ now wholly God, that is in every part immortal.
1.2: 1.2 Who are with me. The Christian brethren grieve over your seduction, witnesses of my truth, whom you ought to believe, and not a few, but all.
1.3: 1.3 And the Lord Jesus Christ. Whom you injuriously equate with the law, while you assert that he is not sufficient for salvation without the law: just as the law without him: but from him, without the law, is grace and peace.
1.4: 1.4 Who gave. That is, offered of his own will: because there is no other who could open the book but the lion of the tribe of Judah. Himself. Because there was no other victim worthy for blotting out our sins, which is the beginning of salvation. What place then has the law? As if to say: None at all. From the world. That is from conformity to the world, which allures us. From this present wicked world. The more it takes hold, since eternal things are not seen. Wicked world. He says this not because this world created by God is evil, but because evils are done in it. And in this sense it is said: The days are evil. The world is seated in the wicked one. Dangerous times. Forest passes full of robbers, and the sword with which blood is shed, and the cup in which poison is mixed, are called evil: because not only times, but also places and instruments of evils have drawn infamy from the things done in them.
1.5: 1.5 To whom be glory. As if to say: The good now present bear witness to this, and those to come will bear witness. In this salvation he gave a foretaste both of his own commendation, and of what the grace of God can do, and that the law confers nothing.
1.6: 1.6 I wonder. The Apostle consequently treats of the destruction of the law. And he rebukes them for fickleness, that they passed indiscriminately from the Gospel to the law. And because Galatia means translation, he fittingly takes from the very name an occasion of rebuke. And since these good things aforesaid are from Christ, I wonder that, well instructed before, you are so, so vehemently and in so short a time, transferred, etc.
1.8: 1.8 But though we, etc. A good angel may be understood, not that this happens, but he is so certain of the truth of his Gospel that if even an angel should announce otherwise, he would not believe but would anathematize. Besides that. AUGUSTINE. Attend. He does not say: More than you have received. For if he said that, he would prejudge himself, who desired to come to some to whom he himself wrote: as to the Thessalonians, that he might supply what was lacking to their faith. But he who supplies adds what was lacking; he does not take away what was in it. But he who goes beyond the rule of faith does not advance on the way, but departs from the way. Let him be anathema. Why this? Because he who preaches otherwise wishes to flow from his own, not from the common source. And since a man hindered by a carnal mist and led back from the common fountain to his own falsity can do this, can an angel not also? Truly, if an angel flowing from his own had not been heard in paradise, we should not have been hurled into death. The commandment of God was set in the midst for all. It was in a way public water, and flowed without fraud, without stain, without mud. But the angel came, fallen from heaven, made a serpent, because he already desired to spread his poison by guile, and sent forth the poison. He spoke from his own, from himself: Taste, and you shall be as gods, Genesis 3. And they, seeking what they were not, lost what they had received. Anathema. This word is used for cursed, and is commonly called devotion. For hardly anyone says he devotes himself, unless cursing himself. Whence that: And he anathematized him and his cities, and the name of that place was called Anathema, Numbers 21. Hence it came about that anathema seems something detestable and abominable, so that the victor should carry off nothing of it for his own uses, but devoted the whole to be paid in punishment: this was to anathematize, which is commonly called to devote. The origin of this word, however, is in the Greek language, from the things that, vowed and paid, that is promised and rendered, were set up on high in the temples: and it is said: that is, to set up on high.
1.9: 1.9 As we have said before. He infers from the greater. Since we or an angel would be excommunicated, much more are the pseudo-apostles to be excommunicated.
1.10: 1.10 Now. He says now because formerly, when he said that man is justified by the law, he preached the glory of man as useless, the grace of God as useful. He hints here that those seducers also do this, that they may be praised by the Jews, whom Paul does not fear to offend for the glory of Christ, at whose coming the law ceases. If I yet. Hence some think conscience suffices, so that they care little what another thinks of them; but conscience before God is necessary, conduct before one's neighbor also; which, if carried on more carelessly, harms by example. Hence elsewhere: Please all men in all things, as I also please all men in all things, 2 Corinthians 10. Likewise: Be without offense to the Jews and to the Greeks and to the Church of God, 2 Corinthians 8. Likewise: Providing good things, not only before God, but also before men, Matthew 5. Likewise: Let your works shine before men, etc. Therefore, against rash judges, detractors, whisperers, murmurers, who seek to suspect what they do not see, who seek even to boast of what they do not suspect, conscience suffices. Nor in others, whom we wish to please, let us seek our own glory, but their salvation, that they may praise not us, but God, who made such men; hence: Do not your justice before men, where he rebukes those who so fan their works that they make the praise of men the end of their works, and reckon the same praise as the reward of their works.
1.14: 1.14 And I made progress in Judaism. As if to say: I who before was so strong in those legal things have now left them, and therefore withdraw from them by my example.
1.15: 1.15 But when it pleased. As if to say: It then appears that I had not learned it, nor did I afterwards. Who separated me from my mother's womb. Hence it is read of Jeremiah: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, Jeremiah 1. He therefore who foreknows those who are to be before they are, makes to be whomever he wills to be born, and calls by grace those already born whom he wills that they may be just, as he called Paul by grace to announce Christ. From the womb. The mother is the Synagogue; her womb and her inner chambers are the Pharisees, from whose number he was separated.
2.1: 2.1 Then after fourteen years. From the Lord's passion, when he had been converted to the faith, he came, as Bede shows, writing on the Acts of the Apostles.
2.2: 2.2 And I communicated to them. He shows that he did not have assurance of the Gospel unless it were confirmed by the authority of Peter and the others. Apart, etc. I conferred with them separately, not publicly, lest a scandal to the faith arise for the believers from Judea (who thought the law was to be kept). At that time, when Peter had come to Antioch (although this is not read in the Acts of the Apostles), Paul withstood him to the face.
2.4: 2.4 Brought in secretly. By the Jews. For what the unbelievers could not do by themselves, they attempted through false brethren, whom they had sent in under the appearance of religion, to spy out the liberty we have in the faith of Christ, not to hold it, but by some contention to bring us back from it into the servitude of the law. If the truth of the Gospel were with the Gentiles, they would not remain, but all would judaize. And therefore here, to those to whom he was laying out the assertion of his preaching, he was in no way willing to yield. Elsewhere, however, where it did no harm, for the scandal of the Jews he circumcised Timothy. In all these things he both commends himself and shows that the law is not to be kept.
2.5: 2.5 Not for an hour. He did not yield even for an hour who never yielded. But if he once yielded, how not even for an hour? Why also on account of the false brethren, if he was going to do it of himself? He yielded therefore on their account: what he would not have done of himself: humbling himself to the law, Timothy being circumcised, so that the guile and scandal of the Jews might cease, who were ready to stir up tumult and sedition if he received that son of Judea uncircumcised and ordained him bishop.
2.6: 2.6 Of what sort they were. I do not go back to earlier things, because what is now suffices; but those who seemed to be something added nothing to me. In which it appears that he is not inferior to them. God is proved not to accept persons, because if it were so, I, Paul, previously impious, to whom such men would have added nothing, would not have been. Or else: it makes no difference, but they added nothing to me. Who seemed to be something. That is, of some authority: because they had walked with the Lord and had been present at his transfiguration. They seemed, I say, to these, that is, to the false brethren. Because those who seemed to be something seemed so only to carnal men; for they themselves are not something. Even if some are good ministers of God, Christ is something in them, not they of themselves. For if they were something of themselves, they would always have been something.
2.9: 2.9 Pillars. The Church is called the pillar of truth: which wisdom also built, that is, set up on seven pillars, by which number either the whole body of preachers (since it is usually put for the whole) or the sevenfold working of the Holy Spirit is hinted. They gave the right hands. How did he confer with them and receive their right hands? Because he had the same word as they. The very conference showed the unity of doctrine; otherwise the Church would not believe him who had not been with the Lord. That we might go. That I should be first in the preaching to the Gentiles, as Peter in the circumcision. And as the apostles were associated with Peter, so Barnabas with himself.
2.11: 2.11 I withstood. Paul would not have dared this unless he felt himself not unequal.
2.12: 2.12 For before that certain came, etc. Certain zealots of the law, who venerated Christ and the law on equal terms, fearing whom he did not mix with the Gentiles. If this were all, it would not be blameworthy. As Paul himself sometimes yielded for scandal. But in this there was error, that he compelled the Gentiles to judaize.
2.14: 2.14 How do you compel the Gentiles. Not by the command of a teacher, but by the example of conduct.
2.15: 2.15 We. His authority having been commended, he now begins to argue by reasons that carnal observances are not to be kept after Christ. As if: The Gentiles ought not to judaize, because we, who were strong in the law, know that it does not justify: and therefore, leaving it, we fled to Christ.
2.16: 2.16 But by the faith, etc. He does not say by faith because good works are made void, since God renders to every man according to his works: but because good works are from grace, not grace from works: because faith working through love would work nothing unless the love of God itself were poured forth in us by the Holy Spirit; nor would faith itself be in us unless God gave it.
2.17: 2.17 But if seeking. If we have truly known that we cannot be justified except by passing over to Christ, does Christ allow us to slip back to what we were? If he allowed it, he would surely be a minister of sin to us, that is, of our former state, as he would have been a minister of justice to those passing over to him.
2.19: 2.19 For I through the law. Understood spiritually. I am dead. That I may not live carnally. That I may live to God. Not to myself, but what can I now do for God? because I am with Christ. Nailed. That is, the cross of Christ has extinguished in me the ardor of sin so that I may no longer be stretched out toward it, as one having his hands fastened with nails.
2.20: 2.20 I live. In virtues I have the vigor of working well. Now not I. That sinner, who I was before. But Christ lives in me. That is, the newness of Christ appears in me. Why then the law?
3.1: 3.1 O senseless. AMBROSE. The words of one in anger. The Galatians were senseless, who did not recognize that they were being circumvented by the false apostles. Has bewitched. A bewitching is when by magical delusions things are shown to men's eyes otherwise than they are. The common name for bewitching is also given to what harms infants. For some are said to have eyes that burn with their gaze, and this act of theirs is called fascination: and it can happen that demons serve this sin. Similarly envy burns like a bewitching. For the envious man harms not only himself, but also those in whom some goods begin to be; hence Solomon: The bewitching of malice obscures good things, Wisdom 4. So it came about that the envious, like bewitchers, harmed the Galatians, newly reborn in Christ, so that the same Galatians, with the stomach of faith nauseated, vomited up the food of the spirit. Before whose eyes. Truly bewitched, because before your eyes, that is, in your presence, he who is so great, Jesus Christ, has been set forth as proscribed. That is, disinherited: and this in you; in others you ought not to suffer that he lose his kingdom and inheritance, much less in yourselves.
3.2: 3.2 This only would I learn from you. Having admonished them by rebuke, he proves that the law is not to be observed, because all necessary things come not from it, but from faith: spirit, justice, blessing. As if: Though bewitched and foolish, yet this I wish to learn from you, because it is so evident that even fools can teach it. If there were nothing else, this alone would suffice for proof, since it is agreed that you received the Spirit; but was it from works, in which you never took labor, or from faith, which comes by the ease of hearing?
3.4: 3.4 In vain. He says so because they had already endured many things for the faith, and in the very sufferings had overcome fear by charity. In vain therefore had they suffered so much who wished to slip from the charity which had borne so much in them to the law.
3.5: 3.5 He therefore who gives. Because you received the Spirit not from works, which you never had, but from faith; therefore you can see that I, who had the works of the law, received the power of giving the Spirit and working miracles not through them, but through faith. About him who had been under the law there could be doubt: but by the likeness of these the whole is clear.
3.6: 3.6 To justice. He here calls justice the remission of sins and the observance of a good life.
3.8: 3.8 Foreseeing. Not only justice from faith, but also blessing, because Scripture says: In you shall be blessed, that is, in conformity to your faith. Because from faith. Not from works, etc. Announced beforehand, that is, showed. Or, announced beforehand, that is, showed it to have been announced beforehand that they shall be blessed in eternal beatitude. In you. In imitation of your faith, etc.
3.10: 3.10 For as many, etc. This is to be understood not of works that belong to morals, but of those that were done in those observances. The law written on tables is profitable: the rest is a burden, which he proves by the authority of Scripture, saying: It is written. They who are of the works of the law are under a curse, for as it is written by Moses in Deuteronomy, Deuteronomy 21: Cursed is every man, etc. As if: I commanded many things, which no one will be able to fulfill: but they were given as a burden, and therefore all are cursed. In which he hints that a Savior is to be desired, who may put an end to these and free us not only from other sins but from the curse of the law. Why then do the Galatians pass from grace to the curse?
3.11: 3.11 Is justified with God. He who worships him freely, namely, not from cupidity of seeking something from him besides himself, nor from fear of losing. For in him alone is our true beatitude, and it is perfect.
3.12: 3.12 But the law, etc. From faith is justice and life: but the law is not of faith. It might indeed seem that the works of the law were done from faith, so that eternal things were hoped for through them: but this is not so, since the Jews kept them from fear of punishment. He shall live in them. He does not say: He who shall do it shall live in it, when he had premised: the law is not of faith; so that you may understand that the law is here put for the very works which were done in those observances. Those who lived in these works feared at least (if they had not done them) to suffer stoning, or the cross, or something of the kind. He therefore who shall do them shall live in them: not with God, that is, he will have a reward, that he may not be punished by this death. But he who lives by faith, when he has departed hence, will then more have the most present reward. He does not therefore live by faith who either desires or fears the present things that are seen: because the faith of God belongs to invisible things.
3.13: 3.13 Being made for us, that is, reputed not only accursed, but a curse. Or, he was made accursed in truth of fact, that is, mortal. Cursed is he that hangs. As if: It is enough for punishment that the guilty man dies hanged: and that he is there until evening, to be taken down and buried then, lest if he be there longer, the reproach be greater, and a stain on his race. Every man. Even Christ, lest future heretics deny his true death.
3.17: 3.17 Now this I say. God promised this to Abraham, and this testament confirmed by oaths, I say and affirm, the law does not make void, of which it should not be thought so: because it was given only for a time: because after a long time from the promise made to Abraham the law was given: if blessing had been from it, the men of that time, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, would not have had it. The law does not make void. That is, false: which it would make if the blessing were given through it. For that promise did not say through the law, but through the seed. For if the blessing is through the law, then he promised in vain to the seed, and the seed itself came in vain. The law does not make void as if it were now able to evacuate the promise: because it would be false, and God a liar.
3.19: 3.19 Because of transgressions. It was set in the midst, between the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made, that is, between Abraham and Christ, to instruct the people of God under the fear of God: that it might become worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ. Ordained by angels. I say the law ordained by angels, that is by Moses and other ministers of God, or given to men by the ministry of angels, in which angels was certainly the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Sometimes, without any distinction of person, God was figured through them. And note that he does not say given, but ordained: as if given in due order between the time of the natural law (by which they were convicted that it could not help) and the time of grace, before they were to be convicted by the law: he therefore who now brings it back acts against the order of the angels. In the hand. That is, in the power of Christ, that the law should stand while he willed, and cease when he willed. You therefore act against him who destroyed it. A mediator is between two extremes, and on this account it might seem either that Christ is not God or that there are two gods. To which he answers, although the mediator is not of one but of two extremes, yet he is one God with God the Father by the divine nature, to whom he mediates through the human.
3.20: 3.20 A mediator. The law which a mediator has belongs to one people only: but yet the mediator himself is not of one people only, that is, the Jews who had the law, but also of the Gentiles, and therefore do not seek the law, that you may have a mediator. The mediator is not of one, but yet he is one: sufficient to reconcile all to God, because he is God, and therefore do not join anything else to him.
3.21: 3.21 Is the law then, etc. Since the law is because of transgression, is it then so against the promises that through it is fulfilled otherwise than was promised: not because from the law there is not life, that is, eternal beatitude: because if life were from it, then justice also: but justice is not from it, but rather it condemns and shuts up under sin. And this is what is said: But the Scripture has concluded. The law itself shut the Jews up wholly under the dominion of sin, and showed all men shut up under sin, as is said also to the Romans: God has concluded all things in justice, that he may have mercy on all. Sins being made known through the law, they are shut up, so that they cannot excuse themselves but seek mercy.
3.23: 3.23 Before. Before the coming of faith the law was useful to the Jews. Faith should come. Faith is spontaneous, which no merit called forth. We were kept. Not free, but servants. Shut up. That thus accustomed we might be led. Unto that. That is, so good a faith. Which. Was at the time of Christ. To be revealed. At the time of Christ many things were opened which were before obscure. Behold the honor of the law: that it kept as a pedagogue: but this is not great, because this belongs to boys, not to adults.
3.24: 3.24 Our pedagogue was in Christ Jesus. By the instruction of Christ: who instituted it so that thus coming to the faith, as boys to perfection, we may be justified. Or in Christ, that is, in carrying out the precepts of Christ.
3.26: 3.26 For you are all the children of God by faith. We Jews at the time of faith have abandoned the pedagogue: because you all Gentiles, who had not the law, are sons. What therefore we have abandoned by your example, do you receive? As if he said: You ought not to do this. In Christ Jesus. In the instruction of Christ, and in the likeness of his death.
3.27: 3.27 You have put on. That is, you have been made conformed to him, which is an honor to you and a protection against heat. That Christ is a garment, the Apostle elsewhere makes clear, saying: Put on our Lord Jesus Christ. Men put on Christ: sometimes up to the reception of the sacrament: sometimes even up to the sanctification of life. And that first is common to the good and the bad. The second is proper to the good.
3.29: 3.29 Then you are the seed of Abraham. Christ is called the seed of Abraham: where it is read that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Here, however, the children of Christ, that is all believers, are called the seed of Abraham. Yet whenever Christ is named the seed of Abraham, it is to be taken bodily: that is, that he is begotten of his stock. But whenever we who believe in him are called the seed of Abraham, then we must take it spiritually as the seed of faith.
4.1: 4.1 Now I say, etc. Now you Gentiles and we Jews are Christ's, and the seed of Abraham and heirs. But once we Jews were under the law while we were little ones, like an heir to come, and one appointed by the father.
4.3: 4.3 Under the elements. By the elements he means new moons, that is lunar days, and the sabbath, not that they hoped in the elements as the pagans, but that in these they worshiped God. Of the world. Because the law promised not heavenly but earthly things: or transitory, as the world is.
4.4: 4.4 When the fullness of time came. That is, after that whole space was fulfilled for which the law was to last, then God sent, etc. The fullness of time. He knew when he ought to come, or even to suffer, etc. For his hour or ours is not, except his will. Yet before, a long series of heralds had to be sent ahead. God sent his Son. Hence, I came forth from the Father and came into the world, John 16. And yet of him the Evangelist John says: He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not, ibid. 1. Then he joins: He came unto his own. He was therefore sent to where he was. Hence also the Prophet says: I fill heaven and earth, Jeremiah 23. It must therefore be asked how this sending is to be understood. If then we think soberly of the Son of God what is worthy, we ought to understand him as sent because, out of that incomprehensible and ineffable secret of the deep majesty, the Word of God gave himself to be comprehended by our minds, not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt in us. Of a woman. The usage of the Hebrew idiom says women, not meaning corrupted ones, but females. Made under the law. That he might appear circumcised as a son of Abraham, having the sign of him to whom he had been promised; in which circumcision was fulfilled: and so let the sign now cease. For Abraham believed he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed: which we believe is now done. That we might receive the adoption. That is, that we might be partakers of the divine glory. For as he by nature partakes, so he adopts us to see it. Hence we receive adoption, because that only-begotten Son of God did not disdain participation in our nature, made of a woman, so that he might be not only only-begotten, but also become the firstborn among many brethren. He says adoption, that we may distinctly understand the only Son of God.
4.6: 4.6 God has sent. For that we might be proved to be adopted by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, who shows the sign of the Father toward the sons, so that since we should not dare to say this through our weakness and unworthiness, he suggests that we dare to say it. The Spirit of his Son. Note that the Spirit is also the Spirit of the Son. And note the Trinity here also. AUGUSTINE. If perhaps someone asks whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son, etc., down to he has it from him, that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from him. Crying. It is to be noted that in the Scriptures crying is understood not as the emission of a loud voice, but of knowledge and greatness of doctrines. Abba, Father. Elegantly he put two words meaning the same, on account of the whole people who were called from Jews and Gentiles into the unity of faith, so that the Hebrew word belongs to the Hebrews, the Greek to the Gentiles. The same meaning of both words belongs to the unity of the same faith and Spirit. Who by nature are not, etc. He shows that the nature of the true God is one, namely of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. What is it to be God by nature, except to be true God? Hence elsewhere the Apostle: You are converted to serve the living and true God, 1 Peter 2.
4.9: 4.9 Or rather known. Scripture often uses this kind of speech; hence: So in the sanctuary have I come before you, to see your power and your glory, Psalm 62., that is, you saw me, that I might see you. God knows us, that is, he gives us the knowledge of himself. For it is not from us that we know him, he knows from eternity: but he is then said to know when he makes things to be known. Weak. Truly the law is a needy element: because it does not justify perfectly. Needy. Because as far as it helps, it does so not of itself, but in respect of grace. Needy elements are called those that need each other to rule the world.
4.10: 4.10 Days. They observe days who say: Today nothing is to be begun. Months. Those who, examining the course of the moon, say: On such a moon nothing is to be begun: these observe and cultivate months. Times. As when they say: Now is the beginning of spring. And years. When they say: It is the new year. But there ought to be no suspicion about these things, because whatever is done simply in devotion to God can turn out prosperously.
4.11: 4.11 I fear for you, lest perhaps, etc. This is observed by those who at certain days, months or years wish or refuse to begin things, as if the times were lucky or unlucky.
4.12: 4.12 Be as I am. I too, who had the law, am now without the law as you ought to be without it. I, I say, who though born a Jew now despise these carnal things by spiritual judgment. For, etc., as you, etc. I am a man who have been corrected from error, and so you can be corrected. Brethren, I beseech you. He consoles those harshly corrected by what has been well done. You have not injured me at all. He excuses himself, because the false apostles had said that Paul was an enemy to the Galatians and had not wished to teach them what he preached in other churches.
4.13: 4.13 Your temptation. For they were tempted (when the Apostle suffered tribulation in the flesh) whether they would desert him through fear or embrace him through charity.
4.14: 4.14 But as an angel of God, etc. He says this because God speaks in his saints, and Paul wished not himself but God in himself to be loved; and therefore he bears witness to some that they received him as an angel of God and as Christ Jesus. In all his saints therefore he is to be loved who says: I was hungry, and you gave me to eat, Matthew 25. Such is the charity of the head toward his body.
4.15: 4.15 Where is then, etc. Admiring their spiritual work, he commends it so that, looking at this, they may not fall into carnal fear. And because they had changed for the worse, he rebukes them. For even if they received him as an angel, he does not on that account spare to cut and burn, because he seeks not his own things but those of Christ. He does not seek milk and wool from the sheep, the same advantage of supplying need and the favor of honor, but the salvation of all. If it could be. Could not what the Apostle says have been done? What is not rightly done cannot be done. He said he could not, what doubtless he could by power, but could not by justice.
4.16: 4.16 Telling you the truth. Because no one wishes to be reproved as erring, and everyone who reproves seems an enemy.
4.17: 4.17 They are zealous. I am not an enemy, but they are zealous, etc. Those are zealous not well who do not so much desire them to be better as wish to make them worse and draw them back by perverse emulation.
4.19: 4.19 Until Christ. Whom you deform, may he be beautiful in you. Or, that he may appear beautiful to others through you. Said more gravely than if he had said they are being formed in Christ.
4.20: 4.20 I would wish. The Apostle, knowing that a speech made to those present has greater force, desires to change the apostolic voice, embraced in letters, into presence. For divine Scripture builds up when read, but profits much more if from letters it is turned into voice. For the living voice has great force, a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, which is uttered with that pronunciation and distinguished because it was generated in the heart of man.
4.21: 4.21 Tell me, etc. Answer. For the sentence hangs thus far. And that is interposed: of whom I again travail, etc. You have not read the law. Whichever they choose, they are proved foolish. If they have not read, they ought not to receive what they do not know. If they have read, the law itself proves that it is to be dismissed. But if they do not understand, they are foolish.
4.22: 4.22 It is written, etc. He had several, but of two only Scripture specially follows out each, hinting that something notable is prefigured in them. One by a bondwoman and one, etc. Nor did he distinguish this in vain: each was born of Abraham, but by a different operation. He who was of the bondwoman was born according to the nature of the flesh, by which a young woman usually conceives from an old man. He of the free woman, not according to the force of the flesh, as an old barren woman from an old man, but by the operation of God, who promised. The one therefore custom begot, showing nature. The other the promise gave, signifying grace. There human use is shown, here divine benefit is commended.
4.24: 4.24 By an allegory. That is said by allegory when something seems to sound one thing in the words and to signify another in the understanding, as here by Abraham, God the Father: for he is the father of many nations. For Abba is father; am, of many. And nations is understood. In Mount Sinai. By mention of such a place the Apostle signifies that the Jews were proud against the Gentiles because of the commandment, or that they themselves were proud and swollen against the commandment itself, which is Hagar, that is, is signified by Hagar. For Hagar means alienation, because it alienates from the inheritance.
4.25: 4.25 Mount. It is joined in all respects and like to Jerusalem, that is, to the Jewish people who now are, that is who serve temporally. The whole people is the mother, individuals are the children, or proselytes, who all serve from fear of punishment. By all this it is plain that the old law is not to be held, but the new, which is above, which is free. Arabia, etc. Humility, or affliction, because they were afflicted under carnal observances.
4.26: 4.26 Which is above. The heavenly city of the saints is above, though in some whom she here bears she is still a pilgrim. Sarah barren signifies that the nature of the human race, vitiated by sin and therefore condemned, deserved nothing of true felicity thereafter. Isaac born by the promise signifies the children of grace: and because this was to be not by regeneration but by generation, therefore circumcision was then commanded when a son was promised to Sarah. For circumcision signifies nature renewed, stripped of its old age. Because it commands all sons and servants to be circumcised, it testifies that this grace belongs to all. Which is the mother. Because each, instructed by her word and example, serves out of charity.
4.27: 4.27 It is written. That she is free and a mother he proves by the authority of Isaiah, adding: Rejoice. To rejoice, to break forth, to cry out belong to liberty. You that bear not. He says this because at that time she had as it were begotten none. You that travail not, because she had not yet made the effort. Rejoice, in the heart. Break forth. Show outwardly the joy of the mind. Cry. Preach your joy to others. For many are the children. This belongs to the mother. Isaiah, looking at the Church of the Gentiles, formerly barren, then fruitful at the time of Christ, addresses her, saying: O barren Church, who in the time of the law bear not even by the power of miracle, etc. Of the desolate. The children of the once desolate Church are more than of the Synagogue meanwhile bearing. It would be superfluous for Isaiah to say this of the old Sarah, so he is to be understood as speaking of the Church. The Church was barren among all the Gentiles before this offspring which we see arose. The Synagogue then is she who has a husband, that is the law. The desolate, however, wandering and living without any power of a husband, is the multitude of the Gentiles, which also was barren, bringing forth the seed of no lawful word. Nature, vitiated by sin, bears citizens of the earthly city; grace, freeing nature from sin, bears citizens of the heavenly city. Who has a husband. The Synagogue indeed had a husband, that is the law, and was once fruitful in children. The barren Church, however, without the husband Christ, without any address of the bridegroom, lay long in the desert. But after the former received the bill of divorce and turned all the husband's ornament to the ornament of an idol, then the husband, the former girdle rotting, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth out of the Gentiles, who, as soon as she was joined to the husband, conceived and bore. Hence Isaiah cries out: Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the cords, Isaiah 54.
4.28: 4.28 Isaac. Laughter, that is those who serve in joy, not from sadness or necessity.
4.29: 4.29 Persecuted. I do not think we can easily find where Ishmael persecuted Isaac, but only that, when the son of the Egyptian was playing with Isaac, Sarah was indignant.
4.31: 4.31 With the liberty. The liberty with which we have been freed by Christ is the remission of sins and the justification of faith working through love.
5.2: 5.2 If you be circumcised. Circumcision and the other legal observances are not harmful to those born and instituted under them, though not necessary; it was more harmful to forbid them as if harmful. The Gentiles, however, are not to be compelled to such things. But if they do not wish to conform to them, like Timothy, they are not to be forbidden; but if they trust in them, they are lost; therefore those observances may be kept by these, lest they seem condemned rather than ended. They are not to be imposed on the Gentiles, lest they seem either instituted without the cause of Christ promising, or still promising; but by ceasing they are now plainly signs of what was to be, which were to be buried with honor, gradually abandoned, not fled from as the sacrileges of the Gentiles.
5.3: 5.3 He is a debtor. He says this so that by the terror of so many innumerable observances written in the law, they might not be forced to fulfill them all, which neither the Jews themselves nor their fathers could fulfill, as Peter says, and might abstain from those to which some desired to subject them.
5.4: 5.4 You are fallen from grace. Which came to this end, that, the burden ceasing, it might justify; and he who brings the burden back loses it.
5.5: 5.5 For we. He who trusts in the law loses grace, which from the contrary can be seen, because from faith is justice, and hope, that is, eternal beatitude: and this we do through the spirit, which cannot be deceived nor deceive. The hope of justice. That is, which justice hopes for, namely eternal life, or, which justice itself is hoped for. For faith hungering and thirsting after justice hopes to be renewed and to advance in it. Or, the hope of justice is Christ, from whom justice itself is hoped for.
5.6: 5.6 For in Christ. For those who in Christ Jesus wish to live piously, virtues are to be sought and vices fled. The middle things between virtues and vices are neither to be sought nor fled, such as circumcision and uncircumcision, which avail nothing in Christ. But faith. Faith without love is empty. Faith with love is the Christian's. The other is the demon's. For the demons also believe and tremble, James 2. Those who do not believe are slower and worse than the demons. But it makes a great difference whether one believes that he is the Christ or believes in Christ. For the demons believed that he was the Christ, yet did not believe in Christ. He believes in Christ who hopes in Christ and loves Christ.
5.7: 5.7 You ran. Here he praises the Galatians and blames those by whom they were induced to wish to judaize; and warns them not to consent to them.
5.10: 5.10 I have confidence. He says he trusts about them because they erred not of their own will but being circumvented. And therefore the true way being now shown, he easily believes they will return. Troubles. That, the order being changed, you may become carnal from spiritual. Whoever. Secretly, they say, he tears at Peter, to whom above he wrote that he had withstood him to the face because he walked not with right foot to the truth of the Gospel: but neither would Paul speak of the prince of the Church with such wanton cursing, nor would Peter be worthy to bear the judgment of the Church. Wherefore it must be thought that this is said of some other, who either had been with the apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed from the Pharisees, or some great one so esteemed among the Galatians that he bears the judgment of the troubled Church.
5.11: 5.11 And I. It was charged by the false apostles that Paul elsewhere preached circumcision, but did not wish to disclose his opinion easily to them. Why do I yet suffer persecution. JEROME. For he endured most frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that those who had believed in Christ from the Gentiles ought not to be circumcised. The scandal of the cross. The preaching of the cross was a scandal to the Jews, because it made void the sabbath and circumcision. If he admitted circumcision, there would be no scandal to them, and they would be peaceable.
5.12: 5.12 I would they were cut off. They trouble you, but would that they were cut off, not carnally, but that they lose the power of begetting in you, or that in others they accomplish nothing, not only circumcised but cut off, so that they have no power of begetting at all, and rightly do I wish this lest they bring you back into the servitude of the law: for you have been called by God to liberty.
5.13: 5.13 Only use not liberty. The sense is: Beware lest, hearing the name of liberty, you think you may sin with impunity. But by the charity of the Spirit. Charity is not to be had through affection of the flesh, but through the spirit.
5.14: 5.14 For all the law. For both those things that belong to good morals and those that are in the sacraments (when they are well understood by the free, and not carnally observed by servants) must necessarily be referred to charity. You shall love your neighbor. This is written in Leviticus, Leviticus 19., in which he rightly says the whole law is fulfilled, though there are two precepts of charity on which the whole law hangs and the prophets, because the love of God is contained in the love of neighbor; and therefore in this precept is the perfection of salvation, because without the neighbor God is not loved: For he that loves not his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he sees not? 1 John 4. Since therefore both precepts are such that neither can be held without the other, it suffices to mention one of them. As yourself. He cannot love his neighbor who does not love himself. And he does not love himself who loves iniquity. For he that loves iniquity hates his own soul, Psalm 10.
5.15: 5.15 You devour. Or accuse, that is, laying crimes on one another. That you be not consumed one by another. Through schism of the Christian religion, through vainglory and vain victory, the occasion of charity being changed, this vice touched them, because dissension is the enemy of love. For by this vice especially of contention and envy pernicious quarrels were nourished among them, by which society and life are consumed.
5.16: 5.16 I say then in Christ, etc. He shows how sufficient is the faith of Christ without the law, because through it they overcome the flesh and its works, and follow the spirit; as if he said: Do not give liberty as an occasion to the flesh, but serve by the charity of the spirit. This I say can be for you in Christ, and never otherwise. You shall not fulfill, etc. He does not say you will not do or will not have, because they could not fail to have them, but you will not fulfill, that is you will not accomplish their works by consent of the will.
5.17: 5.17 For the flesh lusts, etc. The flesh is said to lust, because the soul does this according to it, as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, when rather the soul hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For the flesh lusts nothing except through the soul, but is said to lust when the soul, by carnal concupiscence, resists the spirit. For the cause of carnal concupiscence itself is not in the soul alone, for it is made from both, since without both no delight is felt.
5.18: 5.18 But if you are led by the Spirit, etc. From which it appears that he who is under the law does not have the Holy Spirit, not by dispensation, but truly. You are not under the law. This advantage you already have, therefore this part is to be chosen. He says that those are damnably under the law whom the law makes guilty, not fulfilling the law while, ignorant of grace, they presume on themselves. For he is under the law who abstains from evil from fear, not from love, guilty in will. This law strikes fear, not love.
5.21: 5.21 Shall not obtain the kingdom of God. There is no middle place, so that he who will not be in the kingdom is not in punishment.
5.22: 5.22 Charity. He sent the head first, from which the members follow. For no one rejoices well who does not love the good in which he rejoices. He has not true peace with anyone unless he loves him. He is not long-suffering by persevering in waiting unless he burns in loving. He is not kind unless he loves him whom he helps. He is not good except by loving. Not faithful wholesomely except by that faith which works through love. He is not meek who is not moderated by love. A man does not restrain himself from what disgraces him unless he loves what honors him. Rightly therefore he so often commends charity, as if it alone were to be commanded, which cannot be had without the rest, by which man is made good. Joy. Purity of conscience. Hence: There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord, Isaiah 48.
5.24: 5.24 And they that are Christ's. As if to say: The law is set against the wicked; but for the good the cross is set. Which he says thus: They that are, etc., have crucified their flesh, etc. It befits our devotion that we who celebrate the passion of the crucified Lord should make for ourselves a cross for repressing carnal pleasures. On this cross indeed the Christian ought always in this life to hang, so as to be fixed by the nails and precepts of justice, as Christ was fastened on the cross with nails.
5.25: 5.25 If we live in the Spirit. What he said above in general he turns back upon those to whom he writes, and counts himself among them, by this showing that he does not say to them what he himself does not wish to keep. As if to say: I do not say to you anything that I myself would not do.
5.26: 5.26 Of vainglory. Vain glorying is to wish to conquer where there is no prize. Envying. It is to be known that, since the poison of the ancient enemy is infused into the human heart through every vice, in the zeal of envy the serpent shakes all his inward parts, and in imprinting this malice moves as it were the doorpost. This zeal has no measure, abiding always without end, while other crimes come to an end. And the better the success of him who is envied, the more the envious man burns in a greater fire of the flames of spite. Hence a threatening countenance, a grim look, pallor in the face, trembling in the lips, gnashing in the teeth, raging words, unbridled insults, and a hand ready for violence; and if meanwhile empty of the sword, it is yet armed with the hatred of a maddened mind.
6.1: 6.1 Brethren, and if. Thus far he has spoken to the whole Church, condemning the law and commending grace; now he turns to prelates, how they should treat subjects, namely gently, because they are also brethren, even if superiors. In any fault. Delictum is to turn aside from good, sin is to do evil; or delictum is what is done in ignorance, sin what is done by one who knows. Yet they are used indifferently. Preoccupation is when either for a time it is not seen what is to be done, or he who has seen is overcome so that evil is done when the truth is hidden, or weakness compels. Of meekness. Lest if you act otherwise, he not suffer himself to be rebuked, but begin to defend himself lest he seem base. Considering yourself. Nothing so inclines to mercy as the thought of one's own danger.
6.2: 6.2 And so you shall fulfill the law of Christ. That is charity; for out of charity Christ bore our sins, who also commanded that we love one another.
6.3: 6.3 Nothing. In comparison with the spiritual man, who gives all to grace.
6.4: 6.4 Prove. Let him diligently examine. His own work. Not another's sin, like the Pharisee who said: I am not as the rest of men, Luke 18., who was just not in fact but deceitfully. In himself. That is, within, in his pure conscience. He shall have glory. That is, he shall glory and rejoice. And not in another. That is, in another's praise, namely when another praises him. For he who has the consciousness of a good work ought not to boast of it before another and pour out his praise abroad, but humbly glory in himself. Or thus: And so, that is, if he considers his acts, knowing that no one ought to boast of having a clean heart, in himself, etc. And so in himself. That is, if we consider our acts, we shall prefer ourselves to none, nor judge anyone. The truly just man puts another before himself, because he knows his own evils better than another's, the knowledge of which is his glory. For he rejoices while he knows his disease, which he desires to heal.
6.5: 6.5 For every one. No one is defiled by another's sin. Burden. There are some works of sharing infirmity, of which above: Bear one another's burdens; others of rendering account to God, of which here. Against those who think that a man is defiled by the sins of others, he says: For every one, etc. Against the negligent who care to correct no one, secure that they are not contaminated by others' sins, he says: Bear one another's burdens. We bear one another's burdens of infirmity while with meekness we endure another's anger, and while we pardon him who has injured, if he asks. Or by burden good and evil work is understood. For in the Scriptures burden is taken both in a good and in a bad sense; and so: Every one, good or bad, shall bear his own burden, that is, shall bring back the reward of his works.
6.6: 6.6 Let him communicate. Let him make his goods common to him, and not excuse himself, because God cannot be deceived. It is a customary precept that he to whom the word of God is preached supply the necessities to the preacher, which he rightly marked by the name of goods. As the Lord also in the Gospel, speaking to the disciples, says: When you are evil, you know how to give good things to your children; but foreseeing that some would plead poverty and wish to evade the precept, he added:
6.7: 6.7 Be not deceived. As if to say: Let no one vainly excuse himself, because God cannot be deceived. For he knows your hearts, he is not ignorant of your means. A plausible excuse can please a man, it cannot deceive God.
6.8: 6.8 He that sows in the flesh adds his own. But when he says, in the spirit, he does not add his own, because carnal seed is from man, but spiritual seed is from the Spirit of God. The harvest is promised here at the end. And therefore in sowing perseverance is needed. In the flesh, in the spirit. AMBROSE. The Christian man consists of spirit and flesh. For man in comparison with the Holy Spirit is flesh. But he who sows. That is, who gives to the spirit what is owed from faith, serving justice with charity, and understanding the law spiritually, from the spirit shall reap, etc.
6.9: 6.9 Let us not fail. If man puts no end to the work, neither does God put an end to the reward. As much as we shall have sown in works, so much shall we reap in fruits. And as far as the eagerness of the seeker has been enlarged, so far will the hand of the rewarder open to the reward, because each will receive according as he does; for he who is strong to sow will be strong to reap. In due time. God does not at once do whatever is prayed for unto salvation; nor does he deny because he delays, but he grants in his own time, that is, a fitting one.
6.10: 6.10 While we have time. The time of sowing is the present life in which we run. In this it is permitted us to sow what we wish. But when it has passed, the time of working is taken away; hence: Work while it is day: the night comes when no man can work, John 9. To all. Mercy is to be bestowed on all. In which the just who are of the faith are to be put first. Which the Lord also attests of all our enemies who are wicked, persecuting the Church: Do good to them that hate you. Love your enemies, Luke 6.; for they too are men: on whom the Lord in this sends rain and gives the sun.
6.11: 6.11 See. After exhorting to moral works, he returns to that with which he was dealing before: namely, that legal observances not be held. And lest anyone deceive the incautious under his name, he guards against it by completing the end of the epistle with the annotation of his own hand. For from this place he wrote with his own hand to the end.
6.12: 6.12 These compel. These were the false apostles, who so preached Christ as to teach also that the law must be kept. They preached the cross to make a profit from the faithful; the law, to please the Jews. That they may not suffer the persecution of the cross of Christ, etc. Perhaps he says this because the Roman emperors Caius Caesar and Octavian Augustus promulgated laws that the Jews, wherever they were, should live by their own rite and serve their ancestral ceremonies. For whoever was circumcised, though he believed in Christ, was held among the Gentiles as a Jew; but one who, uncircumcised, showed by his foreskin that he was not a Jew, became liable to the persecutions of both Gentiles and Jews. Those therefore who had corrupted the Galatians, wishing to avoid these persecutions, persuaded the disciples of circumcision as a defense. For neither could the Jews persecute them, nor the Gentiles, whom they saw both circumcising the proselytes and themselves keeping the legal observances.
6.14: 6.14 The world is crucified to me. It happens for the most part that a man does not hold the world in his mind, yet the world binds him in its occupations; and the man is dead to the world, and the world looks on him as if alive, while it strives to snatch him, intent on other things, into its own affairs; but neither does Paul desire the world, nor the world him: so that, both being dead, neither sees the other. Because therefore neither did Paul seek the glory of the world, nor was he sought by the glory of the world, he glories that both he is crucified to the world and the world to him. And I to the world. Neither do I desire anything in the world, nor does it recognize anything of its own in me. As the Lord says: For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing, John 14.
6.17: 6.17 From henceforth. He does not wish tedium to be caused him by turbulent contentions over a matter sufficiently expounded. Or as it is read in the Greek: Henceforth let no man cause or give me trouble, namely, that I should again have need of laboring over you. For he gives trouble to his master who thinks otherwise than he taught. The marks. A stigma is a point or mark made with some iron. He therefore calls them stigmata as the marks of the punishments from the persecutions which he suffered. And the sense is: Therefore no annoyance ought to be made for me, because I have other conflicts and struggles, which contend with me in the persecutions that I suffer.
6.18: 6.18 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. The conclusion of the epistle and as it were the subscription, which he uses in some other epistles also: as if to say: That you may hold what has been said: grace, not dissension, not the servitude of the law, not strife, not quarrelling, etc.
